title: Choosing approved products and prohibited chemicals
audience: Cleaning staff who select or use products on surfaces in healthcare settings.
learningOutcomes: List the six factors the guideline sets for choosing a cleaning or disinfection product.
Name three products or uses the guideline rules out for general cleaning.
Explain why alcohol is not used on large surfaces or on spills.

instruction.heading: Six factors for choosing a product
instruction.body: Six considerations apply. The Therapeutic Goods Administration must have approved the product for that exact use. Its stated purpose has to fit the task. The maker's directions must be achievable on site. The product has to suit the material or room. Trained staff and available resources must be able to use it properly. And it has to act on the target organisms within the time it needs to do so.

instruction.heading: Products ruled out for general cleaning
instruction.body: Strong high-level disinfectants and liquid sterilants are kept out of routine cleaning, because the manufacturer's directions for those hazardous agents rule that use out. Products meant for instruments are never wiped across room surfaces. Large surface areas are not treated with alcohol, which can ignite, and alcohol does not suit spill clean-up either.

instruction.heading: Hypochlorite is a specific-use product
instruction.body: Routine spill work does not require sodium hypochlorite. It can be brought in for special cases once a risk assessment has weighed the setting, the spill, the transmission risk and the surface involved. It stays away from upholstery.

instruction.heading: The label governs
instruction.body: Concentrations, dilutions and contact times come from the label and the facility's approved product list. A product you know well is not automatically approved for the area you are working in, and a product approved for one use may not be approved for another.

procedure: Find the product on the facility's approved list for the area and the intended use.
Read the label for the approved use, the dilution, the contact time and the protective equipment.
Read the label for any surfaces the product must avoid.
Confirm the product does not fall into a category that is ruled out for general cleaning.
Store the product in its original labelled container, away from food and clean stock.
Report any product that lacks a label or does not appear on the approved list.

workedExamples.situation: You want to clean a large stainless steel bench in a clinic kitchen and you have a bottle of high-level disinfectant that a colleague uses on instruments.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Can you use it on the bench?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. High-level disinfectant is not for general cleaning, and an instrument disinfectant is not used on surfaces. Use the approved detergent for the bench, plus any disinfectant the facility has listed for that surface.

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable gloves suited to the product
Eye protection where the label calls for it
Approved product list for the area

commonErrors.error: Choosing a product because it is familiar.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the approved list and the label for the area.

commonErrors.error: Using alcohol on a large surface or on a spill.
commonErrors.prevention: Alcohol is not used on large surfaces or on spills. Use the method the facility directs.

commonErrors.error: Using hypochlorite on soft furnishings out of habit.
commonErrors.prevention: The guideline advises against it. Use a detergent mix for soft furnishings.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A product labelled only for surfaces, or only for instruments, must not be applied to the other kind of item. Working outside the label creates a safety hazard as well as a compliance breach.
Keep high-level disinfectants and liquid chemical sterilants out of general cleaning. Their hazards are specific, and they are used only as the manufacturer and the facility direct.
Ventilate the room as the label directs. Confirm the precautions on each safety data sheet before use.

qualityStandard: Learner names the six factors for choosing a product.
Learner picks the approved product that fits the surface named.
Learner recognises a prohibited use in a scenario.
documentationEvidence: Product log naming the product, its batch and the area used
Record of any product found without a label or listing
summary: A product is chosen on six factors, including TGA approval and fit to the job.
High-level disinfectants, instrument disinfectants and alcohol on large surfaces are not used for general cleaning.
Hypochlorite is a specific-use product, chosen after a risk assessment.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is NOT one of the six factors the guideline gives for choosing a product?
options: The TGA has approved the product for that situation.
The product fits the material or room and the surface it is used on
The product's brand name is well known in the local market.
The product is effective against the organisms concerned

knowledgeChecks.question: Why do large environmental surfaces avoid an alcohol treatment?
options: Because it does not kill any organisms at all.
Because it brings added dangers, flammability among them.
Because it leaves a faint film that attracts dust on the surface.
Because it is slower than detergent on most surfaces.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the guideline say about sodium hypochlorite and soft furnishings?
options: It should be used on soft furnishings every day if the staff ask for it to be used
It is advised against for soft furnishings, which are cleaned with detergent instead.
It is the only product allowed on soft furnishings and it is the cheapest choice for the ward
It should be applied with a steam cleaner at high pressure on every surface
